workflows.title: Understand the Presenter window
The `⋮` button: everything a thing can do
steps: Look at the right-hand end of the row, or the top-right of the card. There is a very faint ⋮ there — as quiet as the colour-note dot beside it, and it comes up to full strength as soon as you point at it. In a list they line up in a straight column down the right edge, each one level with the row it belongs to; a folder keeps its own ⋮ up on its name, beside the ones belonging to the files inside it.

Click it. The menu opens right at the button — the same menu you get by right-clicking the row itself, which still works exactly as before. The menu shifts into view and can use the full window height, regardless of where you clicked. A long menu scrolls only when it is taller than the whole window. Its entries scroll inside it only when they exceed the window's height, or when the menu has its own smaller height limit.
Pick an entry, or click anywhere else to close the menu without choosing.

workflows.title: Switch between the main pages
steps: Click a header tab — the window switches to that page in place. A page has no tab for itself, and the Bible Reader has no tabs at all: come back from it with its 🖥️ [en:tran:Go Back to Presenter] button.

The [en:tran:Slide Editor] tab opens the editor only for a selected slide document: select one in the left list first (W-03), then click the tab; with nothing selected the app shows an alert ("[en:tran:No slide selected]") and stays put.

workflows.title: Present a slide from a document
steps: In the left column, click a document in the [en:tran:Documents] list. It highlights, and its slides appear as thumbnails in the middle [en:tran:Documents] tab. That is the document open; nothing goes on the screen until you click a slide (step 2).
Click a slide thumbnail. The slide goes live: it appears on the mini screen, and the live item is marked highlighted (on-screen indicator).

To step through slides with the keyboard, click once in the thumbnail area, then press →, ↓, PageDown or Space for the next slide, and ←, ↑, PageUp or Shift+Space for the one before. The preview scrolls smoothly to the selected slide, including after several quick Next presses or wrapping from the last slide to the first.

To remove the slide from the screen, press F8 ([en:tran:Clear Slide]) or click the matching clear button (SL) in the mini screen's header. The first card of a PowerPoint, PDF or Word document is blank, on purpose. It is not a page of your document and takes no number: your own page 1 is the card after it, so a five-slide PowerPoint shows six cards. Presenting the blank card puts a blank slide on the screen. What the projector shows is what the editor holds, saved or not. A document you have changed and not saved carries a red * after its name, and the Presenter and the screen show it WITH those changes — the editor keeps your unsaved work on disk. To go back to the saved version press [en:tran:Discard changed] in the editor's row of buttons (it asks first, and it empties Undo as well), then present the slide again.

Show the person on the stage what comes next. A screen's St: number (the badge at the right of its mini screen's footer) decides how a slide is drawn on it, for every kind of document — a slide document, a PDF, a PowerPoint or a Word file — just as it does for a song (W-05): - [en:tran:Stage] 0 — the slide exactly as it is. - [en:tran:Stage] 1 — the slide, with its place in the document in the bottom-right corner (3/12, or Welcome · 3/12 when the slide has a name). - [en:tran:Stage] 2 — the slide at the top, the next slide smaller under it — at full brightness, not faded — and the count. The pair grows to fill the screen's height whatever shape the slides are, flush with its top left corner, no margin, and the slides touch — no gap between them, only each one's frame. - [en:tran:Stage] 3 — the same with the next two slides. - [en:tran:Stage] 4 — the next slide under it, without the count. - [en:tran:Stage] 5 — the previous slide top left, the slide, and the next slide bottom right. As on a song's stages (W-05), the slides around the current one are never faded. On every stage that shows a count, each slide on the screen carries its own — the coming ones too (2/7, 3/7) — in a large figure on a half-transparent dark pill. Set a stage monitor's St: to 2 and the singer always sees what is coming. Moving a screen to any stage above 0 also sets its [en:tran:Slide]: transition to none (W-10). To see it here first, click [en:tran:Add Stage] in the [en:tran:Stage Previewer] header above the slides and pick a stage: it arrives as its own chip and its own pane, side by side with [en:tran:Stage] 0, which always stays. The × on a chip ([en:tran:Hide Stage] 2) takes that pane away again, and [en:tran:Add Stage] brings it straight back. In a narrow pane — beside the Bibles tab, say — the header's title gives way first and [en:tran:Add Stage] folds to its +, so every chip stays in view. There is nothing to set on a document's stage — unlike a song's, its chips have no ⚙. Clicking a slide in any pane presents the same slide; each screen draws it at its own St:.

workflows.title: Auto-play slides on a timer
steps: Open a document's slides and put one on the screen (W-03 steps 1–2) — the stopwatch is only there while a slide of that document is live.
Click the stopwatch icon at the bottom left of the slides previewer — a small strip opens: ✕, play, the seconds box, the countdown, and a sliders button.
Type the interval in seconds, then click play. Slides advance on the timer and the countdown says how long until the next one.

To change how it advances, click the sliders button. The rules open under the strip: - [en:tran:Repeat All] — keep going round. Unticked, the show stops at the last slide and leaves it on the screen. - [en:tran:Step] — how many slides each tick jumps. - [en:tran:Random Up To] — wait a random whole number of seconds up to this, drawn fresh for each slide. The draw is written into the seconds box before each wait, so you can see what it chose. - [en:tran:Wait Until The Video Ends] — clips only (Video Show, and a Videos background list): wait the length of the clip that is up. The seconds box shows that length. Close the rules with their ✕ or the sliders button again.

Stop slides that are already advancing. The timer strip is already open at the bottom left of the slides previewer, in place of the stopwatch. Click its pause button to stop, or its ✕ to stop and collapse it back to the stopwatch.

workflows.title: Present song lyrics
steps: In the left column, click a song in the [en:tran:Documents] list — songs carry a music-note icon. The middle [en:tran:Documents] tab switches to the song view: the lyric [en:tran:Previewer] on top and the [en:tran:Stage Previewer] verses under it. Only one file in the list is ever highlighted, so picking a song releases whatever was selected before. Those two show how the song will look on the screen; nothing reaches the screen until you click a verse.
Click a verse to send it to the screen.
Press F8 / the clear button to take it down.

To attach links to a song — web addresses, or files on this computer written file:///C:/… — open it in the Lyric Editor (right-click the song → [en:tran:Edit]) and add an - Attachments: field to its ol:Config block, one link per line. Each link also becomes its own slide at the end of the Stage Previewer, named after the link. A YouTube link becomes a playable video, an image / video / audio link becomes that media, and any other web address becomes the page itself; each fills the whole slide. Present one the same way you present a verse. A link to a file on this computer works too (written file:///C:/…), which is how a chart or a backing track travels with the song.
Links the app cannot show — a PDF, or a line that is not a web address — still get their named slide, just an empty one.

One song can be previewed at several stages at once. [en:tran:Add Stage] in the Stage Previewer header opens the same menu the mini screen's St: badge does: [en:tran:Stage] 0 to [en:tran:Stage] 5 — a stage already on screen is listed but greyed out — and [en:tran:Increment] · [en:tran:Stage] N at the foot, which adds one past the highest stage you have. Increment is how you get past Stage 5, and it is what matches a screen whose St: number you have already pushed up there. Each stage arrives as its own chip and its own pane, in its own colour; the × on a chip ([en:tran:Hide Stage] N) hides that stage's pane again — its look under ⚙ is kept for when you add it back — and the padlocked [en:tran:Stage] 0 stays.

To change how a stage's slides look, click the ⚙ on that stage's chip (Stage 0, Stage 3, …) in the Stage Previewer header. A small [en:tran:Stage Style] window opens — drag it anywhere, it remembers where you left it. It sets [en:tran:Slide Padding (%)], [en:tran:Background Opacity (%)], [en:tran:Extra Font Size], a [en:tran:Light]/[en:tran:Dark] theme, and a [en:tran:Custom CSS] box for anything else.

These settings belong to the stage, not to the song — every song you open uses them, which is why the panel says _[en:tran:Applies to every song]_. Every stage number keeps its own settings, so you can leave the projected stage plain, make the chord stage larger, and give a third stage a dark theme for the person on the sound desk. Stage 0 is the plain lyrics-only look; every stage from 1 up starts from the chord-and-notes look and differs only by what you set here. Custom CSS is added to the stage's built-in look rather than replacing it, so stage 0 keeps hiding its chords whatever you type. Stages 2 to 5 show what comes next around the verse being sung: 2 the next verse under it, 3 the next two, 4 like 2 in the plain look, 5 the previous one top left and the next one bottom right. The coming verse is at full brightness, not faded, and the verse sits flush in the screen's top left corner with the next one flush left under it, touching it — no margin around them and no gap between them, whatever [en:tran:Slide Padding (%)] says (the padding stays inside each verse's own box). A screen moved to any stage above 0 has its [en:tran:Slide]: transition set to none (W-10).
In that [en:tran:Stage Style] window — the ⚙ on the stage's chip in the Presenter's Stage Previewer — [en:tran:Reset] puts that stage back to the defaults.
A screen already showing a slide keeps it — present the slide again to push the new look out to it.

Edit the words while the song is open and the verses follow by themselves; a verse already on the screen changes when you click it again. Change the song in the Lyric Editor (right-click the song → [en:tran:Edit]) — or in any other window — and within a second or two the rendered song and every Stage Previewer pane show the new words, once the editor has saved them (Ctrl+S): the verses render what the song's file holds. You do not have to re-pick the song. A verse already on the screen keeps its old words until you click it again.

If you ever need to force it — a song changed by something outside the app, say — the ⋮ at the right end of the Stage Previewer header holds [en:tran:Reload], which re-renders every stage at once. The same [en:tran:Reload] sits in the right-click menu of a stage pane and of the rendered song above it. How a song is written: its parts, and the order they are sung in. In the Lyric Editor a song is plain text in blocks. Each part is a block of its own: a line of three backticks followed by ol: and the part's name — ol:Verse 1, ol:Verse 2, ol:Chorus, ol:Bridge — then its words, then a line of three backticks to close it. A chord goes in square brackets just before the syllable it falls on, like [G]. The order it is sung in is its Structure line, in short codes such as V1CV2C, verse 1, chorus, verse 2, chorus. The Structure line, in the first block (ol:Config, beside the song's Title), is the order the song is sung and shown in, so to change the order, change that line — the parts themselves stay where they are. Write it in short codes run together with NO spaces: - Structure: V1CV2C is verse 1, chorus, verse 2, chorus, and x2 after a code repeats it (Cx2). The codes: Verse V, Chorus C, Pre-Chorus P, Bridge B, Intro I, Outro O, Tag T, Interlude L, Instrumental IS; a numbered part takes its number (V2), Intro and Outro take none. The editor marks a mistake in red where it is. It marks a Structure line that is empty, has spaces in it or names a part that has no block (V3 with no Verse 3), two parts with the same name, and a chord it does not know — it knows [Cm7], not [Cm7b5], so write a chord it knows in its place. Put the marked line right and the red goes.

workflows.title: Look up and present a Bible verse
steps: Press Ctrl+B (or click [en:tran:Bible Lookup] in the header). The lookup opens as a popup dialog.

The input is a step-by-step picker. Click the empty box to see the book grid, then click the book, the chapter and the verse. These buttons use the names and numbers of the Bible version you chose, so this is the preferred route for a non-English Bible.

The verse renders in the preview panel. To present it, point at the passage's title (_John 3:16_) — its buttons appear over the end of the title — and click [en:tran:Save bible item and show on screen] (the cast icon), or just press Ctrl+Shift+Enter. The passage is saved to the [en:tran:Bibles] list as it goes up. To keep a passage without putting it on the screen, click [en:tran:Save bible item] (the floppy disk) beside it instead: it goes to the [en:tran:Bibles] list only. The Bible Reader's lookup has the same button. Double-clicking a verse only brings it into view; it does not present.
The dialog closes by itself once the passage is saved, unless _[en:tran:Keep Open]_ is ticked; to close it yourself use the red ✕ button or Ctrl+Q.
Press F9 ([en:tran:Clear Long Text]) to take the verse off screen.

The presented verse also appears in the [en:tran:Bibles] tab (middle column) and the [en:tran:Bibles] list (right column) for re-presenting later. More than one verse. In the grid of verse numbers, click the first verse and then Shift-click the last one (or press on the first and drag to the last); [en:tran:Show all verses], at the end of the grid, takes the whole chapter. Typed into the [en:tran:Bible Reference] box it is John 3:16-18. A passage across chapters. Type it the way you would say it — John 1:50-6:3, John 1-3, John 3:16-4:2 — and present it as above. The projector shows the first three chapters, each starting with its chapter number on a thin rule. On the mini screen card the passage ends with ... ([en:tran:Show the next chapter]): each press puts one more chapter on the projector. The projector itself never shows the .... From the projector window, Ctrl+→ steps to the verse just after the passage (John 6:4) and Ctrl+← to the verse just before it (John 1:49). The next verses, from the projector window. Click the projector window itself and press Ctrl+→ (or Alt+→): the screen moves on by as many verses as it is showing — John 3:16 becomes 3:17, John 3:16-18 becomes 3:19-21 — into the next chapter when the chapter ends, and Ctrl+← goes back. It only works while the main window is on the Presenter: from the Bible Reader, press [en:tran:Go Back to Presenter] first. Nothing on the mini screen card steps the verse; from the Presenter itself, present the next passage the same way you presented this one. Another version on the screen. If no passage is on the screen yet, press Ctrl+B, choose the book, chapter and verse, then press Ctrl+Shift+Enter to present it. On the mini screen card, each column of the passage begins with the short name of its version (KJV, say). Click that name and a list of versions opens. A plain click on one changes that column to it — it adds nothing. To put a second version beside the first, hold Shift while you click it (the list says [en:tran:Shift Click to Add] at its top). With two or more versions showing, the same list has a red row that takes that column away. From the keyboard, highlight a version in that list and press Shift+Enter to add it beside the others.

In a hurry, ask the app instead: open the assistant (🤖, W-42) and type _Put John 3:16 on the screen_ — or the command /verse John 3:16, which needs no assistant. The passage goes up in the version the lookup is on, and the answer says what is on the screen now; it is not saved to the [en:tran:Bibles] list.

To make an editable slide document from a saved passage, first save one if needed: press Ctrl+B, choose the book, chapter and verse, then point at the passage's title to reveal its buttons and click [en:tran:Save bible item] (the floppy disk). Open that item's ⋮ menu in the Presenter's [en:tran:Bibles] list (the right column) and choose [en:tran:Generate Slides]. In the floating panel, tick every other Bible version you want on the same slides — one document holds them all, so this is done once, not once for each version. The original version stays selected. Enter an optional [en:tran:Font Size] in pixels, or leave it empty for [en:tran:Auto]. Choose [en:tran:Dark] or [en:tran:Light] under [en:tran:Theme] to set the generated slides' background and text colors. Both themes retain the translucent, inset background.

Click [en:tran:Generate Slides] in the panel. The new document contains a title slide with the passage and Bible keys, then one slide per verse, with all selected versions together. Each version uses its own configured font. Compact margins leave room for the text; long verses resize to fit, with a consistent reading size throughout the passage, reducing your chosen size only when needed to fit. The upcoming verse appears at the bottom right in muted text at 85% of the current verse's font size. The last slide has no upcoming verse.

Find the file in [en:tran:Documents]. Its name uses the English reference and all selected keys, for example Genesis 1 3-5 KJV-ពគប.ows (the colon becomes a space for the filename). Generating again adds a numbered suffix to preserve the earlier file. [en:tran:Cancel] closes the panel without creating a file. If a selected version lacks a verse, generation reports it without saving a partial passage.

workflows.title: Style the on-screen Bible text
steps: In the [en:tran:Mini Screen] panel, press [en:tran:Reveal Hidden Controls] — the three dots ⋯ at its bottom edge. The buttons under the Mini Screen are hidden until you do, and they stay up while the mouse is on them. The passage in the middle [en:tran:Bibles] tab has the same ⋯ under it, with the same button behind it.

In the row of buttons that came up, press [en:tran:Bible Properties] — the one with a book and a gear. A floating panel opens; there is no card to open inside it, and no separate colour for verse numbers.

Say what is behind the words. The top of the panel shows a verse on a background. Press [en:tran:Dark] when the words go over a dark picture or video — they turn white — or [en:tran:Light] for a light background — they turn black. The look you had is kept and edged the other way round.

Pick a look. Each tile under the verse is two letters wearing it: [en:tran:Normal] is plain words; [en:tran:Thin Outline], [en:tran:Outline] and [en:tran:Heavy Outline] edge the letters; [en:tran:Soft Shadow], [en:tran:Deep Shadow] and [en:tran:Hard Shadow] drop a shadow behind them; [en:tran:Lifted] does both; [en:tran:Glow], [en:tran:Haze], [en:tran:Halo] and [en:tran:Blue Edge] put a soft light behind the words so they can be read over a busy picture. One press changes every screen at once, and the tile in use is ringed.
Change the size. Drag [en:tran:Font Size], or type a number in the box beside it.

Change the colour. Press the small square at the end of the [en:tran:Text Color] row; a colour picker opens under it. Pick a colour and the words on the screen change at once. Press the square again to close the picker.

Change how the words are set. [en:tran:Font Family] is a list of the fonts on this computer: pick one and every verse is drawn in it; pick the first line of the list, --, to go back to each Bible's own font. Letters the font you picked does not have — Khmer under an English font — stay in the Bible's own. [en:tran:Text Style] has [en:tran:Bold] and [en:tran:Italic]; [en:tran:Text Align] puts the lines left, centre, right or justified; [en:tran:Line Height] and [en:tran:Letter Spacing] open the lines and the letters up.

Make a look of your own. [en:tran:Outline] is how thick the edge is; [en:tran:Shadow Blur], [en:tran:Shadow Offset X] and [en:tran:Shadow Offset Y] soften the shadow and move it; [en:tran:Glow] is the size of the light behind the words. Each has a square for its own colour, and picking a colour switches that part on. Somebody who knows CSS can type a text-shadow in the [en:tran:Text Shadow] box instead.

Keep it. Press [en:tran:Save as Preset] — the last tile, with a plus — type a name and confirm. The look, its size and colour included, becomes a tile of its own, and pressing that tile later puts all of it back. Right-click a saved tile for [en:tran:Rename Preset], [en:tran:Replace with Current Look] and [en:tran:Remove Preset].
[en:tran:Reset], at the bottom, goes back to plain words and keeps the size. The font goes back to each Bible's own.

workflows.title: Set the background (color / image / video / web)
steps: Find the [en:tran:Background] panel at the bottom of the middle column, open with its tabs showing. If it has been folded to a thin bar, click the bar and the panel opens again.

Pick a tab: [en:tran:Colors] / [en:tran:Images] / [en:tran:Videos] / [en:tran:Cameras] / [en:tran:Webs]. - [en:tran:Colors]: click a swatch. If the color could clash with the Bible text, the app changes the text color so it stays visible and says so in a message with its own [en:tran:Undo] — it asks nothing. - [en:tran:Images] / [en:tran:Videos]: click an item to make it the live background; click the same item again to take it off. - [en:tran:Cameras]: pick a connected camera device. - [en:tran:Webs]: click a saved page, or use the ⋮ next to the folder path (or right-click the empty list) → [en:tran:Add URL] to add one (a small box asks for the web address; the Web Editor, W-15, is for a page file of your own). A saved address cannot be edited. To change it, right-click its tile → [en:tran:Remove URL] (it asks first, and is not offered while that page is on a screen), then [en:tran:Add URL] with the new address — on the tab's ⋮ at the right of the folder path, or a right-click on an empty part of the list.
The live background's tab carries the on-screen dot before its name (e.g. ● Videos).
Press F7 ([en:tran:Clear Background]) to remove it.

workflows.title: Play audio, and foreground extras (countdown, clock, marquee bottom…)
Show a song in several languages for everyone to sing (Long Text Show)
steps: Open the [en:tran:Foreground] tab and choose [en:tran:Long Text Show] in the menu. Its panel opens.

Add the languages. Press [en:tran:Add Language] and pick one; press it again for the next. Each language gets a card of its own, named by its code (KM, EN), and a language can be in the list only once. The top card is the left column on the screen; the arrows on a card move it, and its ✕ takes that language out.

Give each language its words, one of two ways, chosen on its card: - [en:tran:Raw Text] — type a [en:tran:Title], then one box per section (a verse, a chorus). [en:tran:Add Section] adds the next box; the ✕ beside a box removes it and the arrows move it. A line break in a box is a line break on the screen. - [en:tran:Lyric File] — press [en:tran:Choose Lyric] and pick one of the songs in your Documents list. The card then says the song's title and how many parts it sings. The words come from the song in the order it is SUNG, so a chorus sung three times is there three times. Chords are left out, and so is a part that has chords and no words (an intro, an instrumental).

The languages have to line up. Until they do, [en:tran:Show Long Text] stays off and the panel says the first thing that does not match: typed languages need the same number of sections, none of them empty, and two songs need the same parts in the same order. It reads like this: _The songs do not have the same structure: 1. KM Verse 1 ≠ EN Intro_.

Tick the screen in the Mini Screen panel and press [en:tran:Show Long Text]. Each language is a column under its title and each section is a numbered row, so a verse sits beside its translation. It takes the place of a Bible passage or a slide on that screen.
Let it scroll. On the Mini Screen card, press the double arrow at the bottom right of the picture: the text starts moving up by itself, on the screen too.

Jump to a part. Every card lists its parts as buttons — 1 Verse 1, 2 Chorus … on a song, the section's own number on typed text. While the text is on a screen, press one and that row is marked, faintly, and brought to the middle of the screen in every language. The button you pressed stays lit, on every language's card, so the panel shows where the song has got to. A chorus sung twice has two buttons, and each goes to its own row. On a song's card each part starts as a card holding that part's words, run on in one line with a slash between its lines, for following the song by its words — press anywhere on a card to bring it to the middle. The first button of that row, [en:tran:View as Text Cards], turns them into small buttons with only the part's name, and back; the card remembers which. Step with the keys. Once you have pressed a part, its button has the keys, the way the slides do: Space, →, ↓ or Page Down presses the next part's button, and Shift+Space, ←, ↑ or Page Up the one before. The light and the keys move along with it, on the card you pressed, so you can follow the song from the keyboard or a presenter remote. It stops at the last part, and at the first: it never goes round to the beginning. A part that is not lit keeps its own keys — Space presses that one.

Give a language its own look. Open [en:tran:Properties] on its card: [en:tran:Font Family], [en:tran:Text Color], [en:tran:Text Size (%)] (its size beside the other languages — 80 makes it a little smaller) and [en:tran:Text Align]. A change reaches a showing text about half a second after you stop. Whatever you leave alone follows the screen's own Bible text style.
Change the words. Edit a card and press [en:tran:Show Long Text] again: what is on the screen is the text as it was when you last pressed it.
Take it down. [en:tran:Hide Long Text] beside the show button, or [en:tran:Clear Long Text] (the LT button) or [en:tran:Clear Foreground] (FG) on the Mini Screen card.
The tabs at the top of the panel keep several texts — a song a tab — each with its own languages and looks.

workflows.title: Control what the audience sees (mini screen + clears)
Read the Bible (references, text size, history, versions)
steps: In [en:tran:Bible Reader], click the [en:tran:Bible Reference] box at the top. If it already contains a reference, click [en:tran:Clear input]. Click the book, then the chapter, then the verse from the buttons that appear; the passage opens. This is the preferred route for a non-English Bible because the buttons use that Bible's own names and numbers.

If the words are too small, click the small ⋯ at the bottom-left of the passage to open the hidden controls. Then press and hold the [en:tran:Font Size] slider, move it to the right, and let go when the words are large enough.
To read two Bible versions side by side in one pane, click [en:tran:Add Extra Bible] beside the version name, then click the version you want.

Panes that share a color scroll together. In the Bible Reader, click the dot at the start of the passage pane's header ([en:tran:Color Note]) and pick a color. Point at that header to reveal its buttons, click [en:tran:Split Horizontal to] or [en:tran:Split Vertical to], then choose another Bible version. The new pane joins the same color group. Scroll either pane: the other version follows the same verse. If it does not follow, turn on [en:tran:Sync group scrolling] with the small up/down arrows directly below the color dot. The color, sync-scroll and audio icons are dimmed until you hover over their group or reach one of them with the keyboard. It starts enabled: scroll any pane and the other translations move along with it, smoothly and continuously, keeping the same verse at the same height. When it reaches the top or the end of the passage, they reach theirs too. Scroll another member to make it lead; the others glide into line with it instead of jumping. Click the arrows in any member to turn following off for the group; the previous scrolling behavior remains. Click again to turn it on: the group immediately glides into line with the pane where you clicked, without needing another scroll. The choice is remembered for that color group, and the toggle appears only while the group has at least two panes. Every pane has a color — lime until you pick another. Its two split buttons, in the row that appears while the mouse is over its header, read [en:tran:Split Horizontal to] and [en:tran:Split Vertical to]: click one, then click a version in the list, and the same passage opens beside (or below) it in that version, in the same color group. Panes left on the default lime are one group already, so they follow the same passage and scroll together until one is given a different color; [en:tran:No Color] (or clearing the color) returns a pane to that lime group. A pane that was NOT split off another — a passage dragged onto the edge of a pane from the [en:tran:Bibles] list, a recent reference row or a search result, or one opened with [en:tran:Open beside the current verse] — starts in a color no pane is using yet, so it keeps its own passage instead of following the lime group.

If you lose a passage, you do not need to remember and type it again: the recent reference rows near the top keep it. Click one to read it in a small floating panel, in the version it was read in; the passage you are on stays as it is. To go back to it, open that row's ⋮ (or right-click it) and choose [en:tran:Set to current editing]. [en:tran:Open beside the current verse] in the same menu opens it next to the passage you are on instead.
To change the main Bible version, click its short name in the header and choose a version from the list.
To read without the side panels, click the small ⋯ at the bottom-left if the footer is hidden, then click [en:tran:Full] at the bottom-right. Click [en:tran:Exit Full] to bring the panels back.

The Bible Reader does not put a verse on the audience screen: double-clicking a verse here only selects it. (A double-click means pressing the left mouse button twice quickly in the same place.) To show a verse to the audience, go back to the Presenter and present it from there (W-06). To keep a verse for later, point at the top right of the Bible Lookup and click [en:tran:Save bible item] (the floppy disk), or press Ctrl+Enter: it goes to the [en:tran:Bibles] list, ready to present from the Presenter.

To let supported passages start their generated audio automatically, open [en:tran:Setting] → [en:tran:AI Providers]. After an OpenAI API Key is saved, turn on [en:tran:Auto Play Audio AI when available] under the OpenAI key. The switch lives with the provider setting, not in the Bible Reference toolbar.

workflows.title: Search the whole Bible (Bible Find)
steps: In the Bible Reader (or the lookup dialog), click [en:tran:Advance Bible Lookup] (the binoculars at the top right of the lookup) to open [en:tran:Advance Lookup], the rightmost horizontal section beside [en:tran:Bible and Notes] and [en:tran:Bible Lookup]. Choose [en:tran:Find] in its dropdown; it remembers the last study view used. The binoculars mirror the section's open/closed state. Close or resize it with its divider just like the other sections, and click its collapsed [en:tran:Advance Lookup] strip to reopen it. The toolbar stays available above the sections, even with [en:tran:Bible Lookup] collapsed.

Type your search words. Every verse containing them is listed, with the word you searched for marked in each one, so you can see at a glance why a verse is there. The reference — _Psalm 23:1_ — leads each result; clicking anywhere on the result opens that verse in a small floating panel, in the version you searched, and the passage you are reading stays as it is. Its ⋮ menu has [en:tran:Open], which does the same, and [en:tran:Open beside the current verse], which opens it as a passage beside the one you are reading.

The bar under the results, at the bottom of the panel, says how many verses matched — 74 [en:tran:verses found]. Use it to judge whether to narrow the search: a common word runs to tens of thousands. If a completed search has no matches, the panel says [en:tran:No verses found]. Try different words or widen the book filter. To clear the search and start again, empty the words in the search box: the panel then shows [en:tran:No data available], ready for new words.

Results arrive in blocks of twenty, each headed [en:tran:Results] 1–20, [en:tran:Results] 21–40 and so on. The numbers at the bottom right move you through them: a filled number is a block already on screen, so clicking it scrolls straight there; a plain number has not been fetched yet, and clicking it loads that block in below. Only the numbers near where you are, plus the first, the last, and the blocks you have loaded, are listed — the rest sit behind …, which is a button: it names the blocks it is holding (_Show pages 4–139_) and clicking it lists them all. On a find big enough to run to thousands of blocks it opens in steps instead, and clicking a … between two steps opens that stretch — so any block is a click or two away without the app ever drawing a thousand numbers at once.

To search part of the Bible only, in the [en:tran:Find] view of step 1, click the [en:tran:All Books] button and pick a book — Shift-click to pick several, or choose [en:tran:Old Testament] / [en:tran:New Testament] for a whole half. Once a filter is on, the button shows a funnel and the books you chose; while it says [en:tran:All Books] it stays plain, so a narrowed search never hides in plain sight. The ⋮ [en:tran:More Options] button beside it offers [en:tran:Reset Selected Books] to go back to the whole Bible, and [en:tran:Reset Search Data], which rebuilds the search index — that one takes a moment and reloads the app. To put a result on the screen. Search in the Presenter's Bible Lookup — open it with [en:tran:Bible Lookup] at the top of the Presenter, or Ctrl+B — because the Bible Reader puts nothing on the audience screen (W-11). There, open its search with the binoculars and [en:tran:Find], as in step 1, and type your words. A result has no show button of its own. Open its ⋮ menu and choose [en:tran:Open beside the current verse] — it opens as a passage in the lookup — then, in the Presenter, point at that passage's title and press the cast icon, [en:tran:Save bible item and show on screen], as for any passage (W-06 step 3).

Cannot remember the words exactly? Press [en:tran:Find a Verse with the Assistant] — the robot at the right end of the [en:tran:All Books] row. The help window opens a chat of its own and asks Which Bible should I search?, the one Find is on first. Press one, then type what you remember: a few of its words in any order — _love enemies pray_ — or what the verse is about — _Jesus asked Peter three times if he loved him_. The assistant searches that Bible, and the internet when it cannot place the verse there, and quotes only verses it found in YOUR Bible; under its answer each one has Open … in Bible Lookup, which opens it in the lookup and puts nothing on a screen. Say more under the answer — _no, it was about sheep_ — and it searches again. Under every answer, Show in another Bible — Search another Bible when nothing was found — lists the other Bibles on this computer: press one (English, say, when you were searching a Khmer one) and the verses found are shown from it, or what you typed is searched in it, with nothing to type again; the search then goes on in that Bible. With no assistant set up, the window searches your words itself and lists the verses that hold the most of them, with Search Google for it. You can also just ask in the help window, in any chat: _which verse says do not worry about tomorrow?_ — or in one line, Help me find a Bible verse in "KJV": love your enemies. Typed your words in Find first? Press the robot then, and it searches them at once in the Bible Find is on — no question about which Bible. A story works too. Ask _where in the Bible is the story of the flood?_ — or tell the finder _the story of David and Goliath_ — and the answer says where it is told first, _told in 1 Samuel 17_, with a button that opens that whole chapter, then its key verses. Name the book if you remember it — _in Genesis, Noah and the dove_ — and only that book is searched; it is understood even spelt a little wrong. Every verse with a word. Look for one word — _shepherd_ — and the answer says how many verses have it and in which books. Press Every verse with these words to see them eight at a time, the chapters where the word gathers first, and More verses for the next eight.

workflows.title: Cross references
steps: In the bible lookup, click [en:tran:Advance Bible Lookup] (the binoculars, top right) to open the side panel, then pick [en:tran:Cross Reference] from the panel's dropdown — the second entry, after [en:tran:Find]. You can also get here from the verse itself: right-click any verse in the lookup body and choose [en:tran:Open in Cross Reference]. That opens the panel on this view AND on that verse. Until you have picked a verse the view says [en:tran:No verse selected] and tells you what to do about it.

The top of the view shows the verse it is working from — its version, its reference and its text, exactly as [en:tran:Resources] shows it. Click the reference to move to another verse, or the version chip to read the references in another translation.

Under it, AI [en:tran:Cross References] with the version it is quoting on the right, and a line saying how much there is: 7 [en:tran:Themes] · 35 [en:tran:Verses]. Click the title to collapse the whole section; right-click the title (not the references under it) for [en:tran:Refresh], which re-fetches.

The references are grouped by theme — a sentence such as _Genealogy from Adam to Noah_ — set flush left, with that theme's verses hanging off a single vertical line beneath it. Each verse gives its reference on its own line and the opening of the verse under it, cut at a word with a single … when there is more. Themes set in columns and reflow to one column when the panel is narrow.

Point at any verse and the line beside it lights up, along with its reference: click to read it in a small floating panel, in the version the references are quoting — the verse you are on stays as it is. Drag it into a list, or right-click it (or press its ⋮) for the usual verse menu: [en:tran:Open] does what a click does, and [en:tran:Open beside the current verse] opens it as a passage beside the verse you are on. The keyboard reaches the same rows — Tab to one and press Enter. The version at the start of the panel's title — (KJV) — is a button: click it and choose another Bible, and the same verse opens in a second panel of its own, so the two can be read side by side. Close a panel with its ×.

The chip button on the section title ([en:tran:Generated using AI technology.]) says a model wrote these; click it for the page explaining what that costs you in accuracy. On a translation whose theme headings were machine-translated, each heading carries its own translate button ([en:tran:Generated using Google Translate.]) saying so — on an English bible nothing was translated and the mark is absent.

If you have put your own OpenAI or Anthropic key in Settings, Custom OpenAI and Custom Anthropic appear as their own sections below, each collapsing and refreshing the same way. The section above them needs no key.

workflows.title: Keep Bible notes
steps: Find the [en:tran:Bible Notes] panel. It is a panel, not a tab: it sits beside [en:tran:Bibles] (under it when the column is narrow) inside the [en:tran:Bible and Notes] section — at the top of the right column in the Presenter, on the left in the Bible Reader.
Open a note for editing — the Bible Note editor opens in its own window.

Type your note. Nothing is written to the note file yet — your typing is kept in an editing history, and the row of buttons that appears at the bottom right of the window is how you decide what happens to it.
Press [en:tran:Save] (Ctrl+S) to write it into the note file.

[en:tran:Undo Saved Change] and [en:tran:Redo Saved Change] walk that history — they step through what has been typed since the last save, and they still work after the window has been closed and opened again, so an edit made by mistake can always be taken back. [en:tran:Discard changed] throws the unsaved typing away and returns the note to what was last saved.

workflows.title: Create and edit slides / lyrics / web backgrounds
steps: Select a slide document, then click the [en:tran:Slide Editor] header tab.
Left: the slide list — click to select, drag to reorder. Right-click its empty area → [en:tran:New Slide]; right-click a slide → [en:tran:Duplicate] / [en:tran:Delete].

Canvas: click a box to select it; drag to move; drag the handles to resize; double-click a text box to type into it; Ctrl+Enter focuses the canvas. (From the [en:tran:Presenter], right-click a slide → [en:tran:Edit] ↗ opens this editor in its own window, focused on that slide.)

Add new boxes with the toolbar above the canvas — [en:tran:New], [en:tran:Insert Medias], [en:tran:Insert Media Link], [en:tran:Insert YouTube], [en:tran:Insert Website], [en:tran:Insert Camera] — or the same list from a right-click on the canvas. (The right-hand [en:tran:Canvas Items] tab is a preview/select list, not a place to drag boxes from.) You can also drag items in from the Background panel — see W-28. Insert a video from a link. In the [en:tran:Slide Editor], select the slide, press [en:tran:Insert Media Link] above the canvas, paste the direct video address into [en:tran:Media URL:], and press [en:tran:Ok]. For a YouTube address, use [en:tran:Insert YouTube] and its [en:tran:YouTube URL:] box instead, then press [en:tran:Ok]. Move or resize the new box on the slide and save with Ctrl+S. Insert a camera on a slide. Select the slide in [en:tran:Slide Editor], press [en:tran:Insert Camera], then select the camera's name from the device menu that opens. Selecting a device adds its camera box to the slide. Move or resize the box and save with Ctrl+S. If the app says [en:tran:No camera found], connect a camera and try again.

A website box shows a picture of the page, not the running page. Open Worship takes a screenshot and shows that everywhere you edit, so a service order full of web slides stays fast even on an old machine. Two things follow: - Hover the box for about a second to see the page live; move away and the picture comes back. - The picture does not update itself. If the page changes (a clock, a countdown, a scoreboard), right-click the box → [en:tran:Refresh Preview]. When you actually present the slide, the audience screen shows the real, live page — only your editing and preview views use the picture.

Blend a box with the ones under it. Select a box, and under [en:tran:Shape Properties] in the right-hand [en:tran:Properties] tab pick a [en:tran:Blend Mode] — [en:tran:Multiply] to darken, [en:tran:Screen Blend] to drop black out of a clip, [en:tran:Overlay] for a texture over a photo. It blends with the canvas items underneath it in the same slide, so it only shows where the box overlaps another one; put a picture or video box behind, sized [en:tran:Full], and blend over that. It does not reach the background you attached to the slide. [en:tran:Normal] turns it off again.

Give a box a shadow. In the same [en:tran:Shape Properties] group, pick a [en:tran:Shadow]. There are two kinds and they are not the same thing: - [en:tran:Box Shadow] is the shadow of the box itself — its rectangle, with whatever corner rounding you gave it. This is the one for a text box with a coloured backing. - [en:tran:Drop Shadow] is the shadow of what is actually painted, so it hugs the letters of a box with no backing colour, and the cut-out edge of a logo picture. Giving a see-through logo a box shadow draws a rectangle in mid-air behind it — this is the setting that avoids that. Three boxes then appear: X: and Y: are how far the shadow falls (either way — a negative Y: throws it upwards), [en:tran:Blur:] is how soft it is, and the colour row under them sets its colour and how see-through it is. Keep the blur modest on an old machine: a big soft shadow is the one setting here that costs the computer real work. [en:tran:No Shadow] takes it off again.

Apply a font setting to several items. Under [en:tran:Properties], expand [en:tran:Bulk Font]. Leave [en:tran:Apply to] on [en:tran:All Slides] for the whole document, or pick [en:tran:Choose slides and items]. Tick a slide to select its text items; expand its [en:tran:Canvas Items] list to tick individual items. You can combine items from several slides. A partially selected slide shows a dash in its checkbox. Text, Bible and HTML items are included; media items have no font setting. Locked items stay unchanged unless you tick [en:tran:Include locked items]. Enter a positive [en:tran:Font Size] in pixels and press [en:tran:Apply Font Size], or choose a [en:tran:Font Family] and press [en:tran:Apply Font Family]. Each button applies only that property, leaving the other styles and positions intact. The result reports how many items changed. Each application is one [en:tran:Undo] step; [en:tran:Redo] reapplies it. To change the words' colour as well, select the box and click the hex value under [en:tran:Text Properties] → [en:tran:Color]. Type or paste the new hex color, then press Enter or click away to apply it (step 9).

Type an exact color. Select a box, then click the hex value beside [en:tran:Background Color] or under [en:tran:Text Properties] → [en:tran:Color]. Type or paste a hex color, then press Enter or click away to apply it. Three-, four-, six- and eight-digit hex values work, with or without #; eight digits include opacity, for example #2468AC80. Escape cancels the unfinished edit. Invalid or incomplete values return to the current color without changing the slide. The arrow still opens the swatches and opacity slider. [en:tran:Undo] / [en:tran:Redo] restore and reapply changes.
Save with Ctrl+S.

workflows.title: Remove a song, document or file (Move to Trash)
steps: Find the row in its list — a song or slide document in [en:tran:Documents], a picture or video in the [en:tran:Background] panel, a run sheet in [en:tran:Presenting Flows].
Right-click the row, or click the faint ⋮ at its right-hand end (W-01b). The row's menu opens.
Choose [en:tran:Move to Trash] — the last item, with a red trash icon.
A small window asks [en:tran:Moving File to Trash] — _Are you sure you want to move "…" to trash?_ Click [en:tran:Yes]. ([en:tran:No] leaves everything as it was.)
The row disappears from the list. The file, and any pictures or media that belonged only to it, are in the Recycle Bin / Trash — open that from your desktop to restore them.

workflows.title: Settings: language, theme, fonts, folders
steps: Click the gear ([en:tran:Setting]) in the header — Settings opens in its own window, on [en:tran:Path Settings]. [en:tran:App Assistant] above [en:tran:Apply Settings] at the bottom-left opens the help window, to ask about any setting.

[en:tran:General] tab: - [en:tran:Language]: click English, ខ្មែរ or Français. Each language is listed under its OWN name, whatever locale you are currently in — so if a mis-click leaves you in a script you cannot read, the way back is still legible. (Hover a button and its title gives the English name.) Some labels change straight away, but the switch is only complete once you click [en:tran:Apply Settings] at the bottom-left — that reloads every open window. Unsaved edits in the Slide Editor are kept. The language belongs to this computer, not to the data folder: switch to another data folder and the app stays in the language you chose. - [en:tran:Theme]: system / light / dark. - [en:tran:Font Family]: the font the app's own windows are drawn in — not the text on the audience screen. A font marked (Missing) is configured but not installed on this computer. When the chosen font comes in more than one weight, a second list beside it picks one (400 Regular, 700 Bold…); [en:tran:Default] keeps the font's own weight. - Reset button (Clear All Settings): this erases configuration; use with care. It asks for confirmation first. - [en:tran:Show Tips of the Day automatically]: controls whether the Presenter and Bible Reader show an automatic tip after the next app launch. - Panel sizes are no longer reset from here — see W-31.

[en:tran:Bible] tab: import a Bible XML from a file or URL, edit installed XML Bibles, or export/import a [en:tran:Bible Data] archive. The old online version list is development-only and can be unavailable. An installed Bible has no on/off switch. Every Bible in that list is offered wherever a version is chosen. To stop one being offered, take it off the computer: the trash icon on its row, [en:tran:Move to Trash], opens a confirmation titled [en:tran:Delete Bible XML]. Press [en:tran:Yes] in that dialog to send its file to the Recycle Bin, from where it can be brought back or imported again.
[en:tran:AI Providers] tab: the AI master switch, the provider keys and the custom servers — see W-42.
Click [en:tran:Apply Settings] (bottom-left) to apply — the app windows reload.

workflows.title: Find text anywhere (Find bar) & About
Use more than one screen (multi-screen)
steps: Right-click an empty area of the mini-screen panel and choose [en:tran:Add New Screen] — a second preview card appears with its own number and color.
Point the new card at the display it should fill with the Display button in its footer (W-10), then turn it on with its own show/hide button. Every card has its own clears, transitions and lock too.

Content goes to every selected screen. To stop one screen receiving content without deleting it, right-click its card and choose [en:tran:Deselect], and [en:tran:Select] there takes it back. [en:tran:Solo] does something else. It makes that card the ONLY selected one, so every other screen stops receiving. A screen that is not selected keeps what it last showed, and that, or an item dropped on one card (step 4), is why two screens can show different things. Select every card — right-click one that is not and choose [en:tran:Select] — and present the item again to put the same thing on all of them.
You can also drag a slide, background item, or foreground Show button and drop it on one specific card to present it on that screen only.

A Bible passage shown in more than one version is drawn as one column per version, and the columns keep together: scroll one of them on the card — the wheel, its scrollbar or the auto-scroll button — and the others move to the same verse, on the screen it shows as well. To line the versions up verse by verse, in rows, right-click the card of the screen showing it and choose [en:tran:Set Line Sync] — one screen is all it needs, and a screen already showing takes the rows only once it is hidden and shown again — and [en:tran:Unset Line Sync] goes back to columns. Its scrolling follows the card either way.
Right-click a card → [en:tran:Delete] removes a screen you no longer need (the first screen can't be deleted while it is the only one).

workflows.title: Draw and spotlight on the app itself (Presenting Control)
steps: Open the Tools menu → [en:tran:Start Controlling], or press Ctrl+Shift+P instead (⌘+Shift+P on Mac) — one or the other. Every window of the app answers it — the Presenter, the Bible Reader, the Slide Editor, a Bible Note, Settings, the Web Editor, the Lyric Editor and Local Web Share — and the one you are looking at is the one that gets the panel. (The projector output, the About box and the Find bar deliberately do not: an overlay on what the congregation sees is the one place this must never appear.) The menu bar is hidden on the smaller windows, so the shortcut is the way in there. A floating [en:tran:Presenting Control] panel appears — drag it by its title bar, resize it from any edge or corner, double-click the title bar to fill the window (and again to put it back), and collapse it with the chevron once a tool with settings is showing; it reopens where and how you last left it.

The title bar carries everything you reach for mid-presentation: the four tools on the left, then the keyboard screencast switch (W-20) and [en:tran:Undo] / [en:tran:Redo] / [en:tran:Clear drawing] on the right. Only the settings live in the body, so collapsing the panel with the chevron leaves every group one click away — roll it up to get the sliders out of the way and keep drawing.

The panel opens on the arrow tool — the app stays completely usable and anything already drawn stays visible on top of it. The arrow has no settings of its own, so on it the panel is just its title bar: no empty body sitting over the app you have just asked to have back, and no chevron either, because there is nothing to roll up. Pick the brush, eraser or spotlight and the body opens again at the size you last left it.

Click the brush to draw. A thin teal frame around the window shows the app is no longer taking clicks; drag anywhere to draw. Pick [en:tran:Color], [en:tran:Size] ([ / ]) and [en:tran:Opacity] (- / =), and switch the stroke style with [en:tran:Straight] (S), [en:tran:3D] (3) or [en:tran:Dots] (D). [en:tran:HQ] (Q) trades smoothness for speed on weak machines.

Click the eraser to rub parts of the drawing out, and use the title bar's [en:tran:Undo] / [en:tran:Redo] (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z) to step back or the red [en:tran:Clear drawing] (C) to wipe it — one Undo brings a mis-hit Clear back. All three grey out when there is nothing to undo, redo or clear, and all three keys work from any armed tool (brush, eraser or spotlight) and with the panel collapsed. On the arrow tool those keys go to the app instead, and only the buttons act on the drawing.

Click the spotlight to dim the whole app except a circle. In [en:tran:Follow] (the default) the circle simply tracks your pointer; press the [en:tran:Follow] button itself (H) and it reads [en:tran:Hold], which dims only while the mouse button is down. [en:tran:Contrast] (X) inverts it — the circle becomes the blocked area instead. Size, [en:tran:Dim color], dim amount and edge blur (, / .) all have sliders.

The camera at the end of the title bar takes a picture of the app as it looks right now — your drawing, your spotlight and all — and asks what to do with it: [en:tran:Ask the assistant about this] opens the help window with the picture already attached, so "what is this?" is one press and one sentence; [en:tran:Copy] puts it on the clipboard; [en:tran:Save into your images] puts it in the Background Images folder, where it can then be presented like any other picture. The help window itself never appears in the shot, even when it is sitting on top of the app.
Press Escape (or click the arrow) to hand the app back while keeping the drawing on screen. Move the panel if it covers what you are pointing at.

Click ✕ in the panel header to finish. The drawing is discarded; it is not saved between sessions. Ctrl+Shift+P and Tools → [en:tran:Start Controlling] are a toggle: pressed again while the panel is open, they close it — and the drawing goes with it, exactly as ✕ does. While a drawing tool is armed the shortcut does nothing — the keyboard belongs to the drawing then: press Escape first, or use the menu entry, which closes the panel either way.

workflows.title: Show the keys you press (Keyboard Screencast)
steps: Open the [en:tran:Presenting Control] panel (W-19 step 1: Tools → [en:tran:Start Controlling], Ctrl+Shift+P).

In the panel's title bar, click the keyboard button (K) — it sits between the four tools and Undo / Redo / Clear, and lights up while it is on. Nothing appears on screen yet; the strip only shows up once you press something.
Press any key. A dark strip of key pills appears across the bottom of the window, above everything else — including your own drawing and the spotlight.

The strip keeps the last six keys. Pressing the same key over and over collapses into one pill with a ×N counter (→ ×2), so a run of arrow presses does not push the rest of the strip away. Holding a key down counts as one press.

Chords are shown the way the app names them: Ctrl+Z, Esc, Space, ↑ ↓ ← →. Plain typing shows the character you actually typed; a shortcut is shown on the en-US key the app binds it to, whatever your layout produces.
The strip clears itself about a second and a half after your last key, so it is never in the way between one demonstration and the next.
Click the keyboard button again (or press K) to turn it off. Closing the panel turns it off too — the screencast belongs to the panel, and reopening starts with it off again.

Picking the brush, eraser or spotlight turns it off as well, and greys the keyboard button out until you go back to the arrow — an armed tool swallows the keyboard (W-19), so there would be nothing left to echo. Turn it back on with K or the button once the arrow tool is back.

workflows.title: Add a background video or song from a link
steps: Open the [en:tran:Background] panel (W-08 step 1) and choose the [en:tran:Videos] tab — or the [en:tran:Audios] split if you want the sound only.
Right-click an empty part of the list (or use the ⋮ [en:tran:More Options] button at the right of the folder-path bar) and choose [en:tran:Download From URL].

A small box asks for the link — [en:tran:Video URL:] on the Videos tab, [en:tran:Audio URL:] on Audios. If you copied the link first, it is already filled in; otherwise paste it. The box is only outlined red — with [en:tran:Cannot be empty] under it — once you have typed in it and emptied it again.
Click [en:tran:Ok]. The download runs in the background — a full song or video takes a couple of minutes, and you can keep using the app while it does.

When it finishes, the file appears in the folder you were in: the video shows up as a new thumbnail in the Videos tab, the audio as a new row under [en:tran:Audios]. From there it behaves like any other background (W-08) or track (W-09).

workflows.title: Build a service presenting flow (a running order)
steps: Find the [en:tran:Presenting Flows] panel — it is the lower of the two lists on the left, under [en:tran:Documents]. If the list is empty, right-click its empty area (or use the ⋮ [en:tran:More Options] button in its title bar) → [en:tran:New File] to create one.

Drag things onto the presenting flow's NAME row to add them. The NAME row is the presenting flow's own row in the list — the one with its name on it; not the empty part of the list, and not a line inside an open presenting flow (dropping onto a _line_ does something else — it attaches: see W-22g). So, to add a song or a verse: take hold of its row — in the Documents list, or in the Bible list — drag it over to the Presenting Flows list and let go on the row that shows the presenting flow’s name. It is added at the end. Anything you can present can go in: - a background — a colour, image, video, camera or website; - a document — a slide document or a song (a song is a document too): drag its row out of the Documents list; - a single slide — from the previewer, or from a document already in the presenting flow; - a Bible verse — from the Bible list; - a foreground preset — drag the blue [en:tran:Show Marquee Top] / [en:tran:Start Countdown] / [en:tran:Show Time] button itself. Whatever you typed and styled travels with it, so the presenting flow remembers _that_ announcement, not just "a marquee". - an audio track — drag it out of the [en:tran:Audios] split.

Click the presenting flow name to open it. Each element is one short line: an icon for what it is, its id, and its name. A document line has its own arrow at its left end — a song is a document too. Click the arrow, not the line, to see that document's slides underneath; clicking the line itself opens the document in the previewer.

A song or document line opens its previewer. To present one of its slides, click that slide in the previewer, or expand the document with its arrow and click a slide underneath. An audio track opens the [en:tran:Audios] split and flashes the track there; use that panel's play button to play it. Click a single slide, Bible verse, background or foreground preset to put it on the screen. You can also drag an element onto a mini screen, or right-click → [en:tran:Show on Screens] to pick the screen.

Right-click an element for [en:tran:Move up] / [en:tran:Move down], [en:tran:Choose Color] to group your running order by colour, or [en:tran:Remove from Presenting Flow]. To move a line a long way, use [en:tran:Move to Top] or [en:tran:Move to Bottom] instead of clicking [en:tran:Move up] over and over — the line jumps straight to that end and everything else keeps its order. (A line that is already at the top is not offered [en:tran:Move up] or [en:tran:Move to Top], and one already at the bottom is not offered [en:tran:Move down] or [en:tran:Move to Bottom].) [en:tran:Duplicate] puts a copy of the line directly below it, with its colour, its pinned screens and its parked slides already on the copy — the quick way to sing a song twice in one service, then change only the second one. The two copies are separate from then on: parking or recolouring one leaves the other alone. You can also drag a line up or down inside the same presenting flow (dragging a line into a _different_ presenting flow does nothing — add it there from its own list instead). A colour shows as a stripe down the left edge of the line and a dot at its right end; the lines stay in your running order — they are never re-sorted into colour groups, because the order _is_ the meaning here. The colour belongs to that presenting flow alone, so the same song can be marked differently in two services. Changes are saved as you make them — there is no save button anywhere in this panel.

Whatever is live on the screen right now is marked with a magenta ● — on the element itself, on the document it belongs to, on the presenting flow, and on the [en:tran:Presenting Flows] heading — so you can see at a glance where you are in the running order.

Not sure which "5.jpg" a line means? Right-click it → [en:tran:Reveal Original] — the app scrolls to the real item elsewhere in the window and flashes it. This works on the slides inside an opened document too. A colour or a camera has no original to point at, and the panel holding the original has to be open already.

workflows.title: Run the service from the presenting flow's preview panel
steps: To see the whole service at a glance, click the window icon on the presenting flow row once (or right-click → [en:tran:Open Preview]) — a second click on it closes the panel again. A floating panel shows every element with its real preview — slides look exactly as they will project, and a document shows all of its slides. Opening it puts nothing on a screen, and neither does scrolling it: that is how you look ahead. An element goes up only when you click its preview or press one of the keys below — those keys run the service, they are not for looking. Collapse the ones you are not working on — or fold the whole running order away at once with the [en:tran:Collapse All] icon at the bottom-left of the panel, and open it all again with [en:tran:Expand All] beside it. Whichever of the two has nothing left to do fades out. Whatever you folded away is remembered for that presenting flow, so a running order trimmed down to the few things you are working on comes back that way next time — and it follows the element, not its position, so reordering the list does not shuffle what is folded. To make the thumbnails bigger or smaller, use the zoom slider in the panel's footer (it tucks itself away into a ⋯ button at the bottom-left), Ctrl + scroll, or a two-finger pinch. This zoom is remembered separately from the one in the middle Documents tab — and it is shared by every one of these panels, so zooming one resizes them all. You can have several of these panels open at once, one per running order — the songs in one and the sermon in another, side by side once you drag them apart. Each opens a little below and to the left of the last, so it never lands exactly on top of it; each remembers its own size and place, and is closed on its own with its ✕ (or by clicking its window icon in the list again). Each is its own run, too: where you are, what you have folded away and any countdown belong to that panel alone, and the keys below always drive the one you last clicked into.

Run the service from this panel. Click an element — the panel outlines it and remembers it as where you are. Clicking its preview also shows it, and clicking the title line of a folded element marks it just the same — folding is the chevron on its left, so pointing the run at an element never folds it away. Then Space, ↓, → or Page Down puts the next element on the screen: every press shows the congregation the next thing, so one key runs the whole service. A document is walked slide by slide: arriving at it always shows its first slide, each further press shows the next one, and the keys only move on to the next element once its last slide is the one on screen — so a whole song or sermon deck plays from here without touching the mouse. A folded-away element is not passed over: the run opens it when it gets there, and a song folded away is unfolded and walked from its first slide like any other. Folding is how you _read_ a long running order; it never decides what is in the service. The only line the keys step over is one you have parked (W-22i) — an audio track and a damaged line still take the marker, so you can see where the run has got to, they simply have nothing to show. The last element is the end — it does not start over. The keys work while you are in this panel, and it takes them the moment you open it, so there is nothing to click first; click into the slides list and they drive that list again, as before. Clicked somewhere else and the keys stopped? Press the key three times quickly and this panel takes them back (W-49b).

A screen action is stopped on and fired like anything else (W-22c) — so putting a [en:tran:Clear All] between the last song and the sermon means one more press of the same key blanks the screen at exactly that point in the running order. The Next: lines are fired the same way, and what they fire is this panel: a wait that moves the run on by itself (W-22d), or a loop that keeps moving it (W-22e).

Everything you can right-click in the list, you can right-click here. The menus in this panel are the very same menus — right-click an element's title line (or any empty part of its box) and you get its full menu: [en:tran:Reveal Original], [en:tran:Show on Screens] / [en:tran:Apply on Screens], [en:tran:Set Specific Screen], [en:tran:Add CC Elements], the four moves, [en:tran:Duplicate], [en:tran:Choose Color], [en:tran:Disable] / [en:tran:Enable] and [en:tran:Remove from Presenting Flow], gated exactly as they are in the list. So you can tidy and re-order the running order from the panel you are actually watching during the service, without going back to the list — and the list behind it follows immediately. Two things inside a box keep menus of their own, because they are not the element: a slide thumbnail gets the slide's menu ([en:tran:Reveal Original], [en:tran:Show on Screens], [en:tran:Set Specific Screen], [en:tran:Disable], [en:tran:Add CC Elements], [en:tran:Add Media Control]), and a CC line gets its short one ([en:tran:Reveal Original], [en:tran:Set Specific Screen], [en:tran:Remove CC Element]).

workflows.title: Clear the screen, or show and hide it, from a running order
steps: Add a screen action. A running order can also hold something to _do_ rather than something to show. Right-click the presenting flow itself — its own row in the list, not the empty part of the list and not one of its lines — and choose [en:tran:Add Action]: every action is added from that one menu. For a clear, pick [en:tran:Clear Screen] there — a row that adds nothing and opens the clears — and then one of [en:tran:Clear All], [en:tran:Clear Background], Clear Slide ([en:tran:Clear Slide]), [en:tran:Clear Long Text] or [en:tran:Clear Foreground] — the same five clears as the buttons on each mini screen, and the line carries the same ALL / BG / SL / LT / FG badge so you can tell them apart at a glance. It lands at the end of the list; drag it up to where it belongs — say between the last song and the sermon. Under those five, [en:tran:Other Clear FG Items] offers a finer clear for one foreground widget at a time, so you can take the countdown down and leave the marquee running: [en:tran:Clear FG Messages] (MS), [en:tran:Clear FG Marquee Top] (M↑), [en:tran:Clear FG Marquee Bottom] (M↓), [en:tran:Clear FG Quick Text] (QT), [en:tran:Clear FG Countdown] (CD), [en:tran:Clear FG Stopwatch] (SW), [en:tran:Clear FG Time] (TM), [en:tran:Clear FG Video Show] (VD), [en:tran:Clear FG Image Show] (IM), [en:tran:Clear FG Camera Show] (CM), [en:tran:Clear FG Screen Show] (SS) and [en:tran:Clear FG Web Show] (WB). Each does exactly what that widget's own hide button in the [en:tran:Foreground] panel does; the Messages, Time, Video Show, Image Show, Camera Show, Screen Show and Web Show ones clear all of their items at once.

A screen action is run, not shown. Click it to clear, drag it onto one mini screen to clear only that one, or right-click → [en:tran:Apply on Screens] to choose. It never lights up as "live", because there is nothing of it on the screen to be live. In the preview panel (W-22b) it is stopped on and fired like any other line — so a [en:tran:Clear All] between the last song and the sermon means one more press of the same key blanks the screen at exactly that point in the running order.

Put the screen itself up and down. Two more actions are not about what is _on_ a screen but about whether there is one: [en:tran:Screen: Show] and [en:tran:Screen: Hide], the same thing the slides button on each mini screen does by hand. Use them when the running order has to work with nobody at the machine — a [en:tran:Screen: Show] at the top of a pre-service loop, a [en:tran:Screen: Hide] at the end of it, and the screen goes dark on its own instead of holding the last announcement until someone notices. These two ask which screen when you add them, and that is the whole point: a checklist of the screens you have open appears (Screen id: 0, Screen id: 1, …, each in that screen's own colour), and the line remembers your answer as its pin — the line shows the pin badge, and [en:tran:Set Specific Screen] re-aims it later. Unlike every other line, it goes to those screens and _only_ those: it will not fall back to whichever screen you happened to have selected, and it will never stop to ask, because at 7:05 on an unattended sheet there is nobody there to answer. Tick nothing and the app says [en:tran:Please choose at least one screen] rather than adding a line that would do nothing. Like every action, the line lands at the end of the list: drag it up to where it should fire. Firing one twice is harmless — a [en:tran:Screen: Show] on a screen that is already up does nothing at all, so it is safe inside a loop. Nothing can be attached to them either, though they can themselves be attached to another line — "put this last slide up and light the screen" in one click. Clicking one goes to the screens it names and nowhere else; [en:tran:Apply on Screens] still asks, since that entry is you saying "send this one somewhere else" — but it does not change what the line is pinned to.

Where the actions live in the menu. [en:tran:Add Action] opens with [en:tran:Clear Screen] — one row that adds nothing and opens the five clears, with [en:tran:Other Clear FG Items] under them for the twelve per-widget foreground clears — then [en:tran:Screen: Show] / [en:tran:Screen: Hide], then the five that drive the run.

workflows.title: Make a running order wait, then move on by itself (Next: Timeout)
steps: Let the running order walk itself. In the [en:tran:Presenting Flows] list (not in the preview panel), right-click the presenting flow itself — the row with its name on it, not the empty part of the list and not one of its lines — and choose [en:tran:Add Action] → [en:tran:Next: Timeout]. That adds a NEW line to the running order; it is never added by right-clicking a line that is already there. It goes at the END of the running order: drag it up to just after the line it should follow. It asks how many [en:tran:Seconds], and the answer is part of the new line — ⏱ Next: Timeout (5) — so a glance at the sheet tells you how long it waits. Got it wrong? Right-click that Next: Timeout line → [en:tran:Change Timing]; it opens on what it is holding now.

[en:tran:Next: Timeout] waits once. When the run reaches it, it counts down and then moves the run on by itself — a slide that should linger ten seconds and then go on without you. Going somewhere yourself calls it off: click another line, or press the next key, and the wait is over and you are driving again. A click that goes nowhere does NOT call it off: clicking a background or a foreground button, or a stray click on the panel, leaves it counting, so a mis-aimed click cannot silently cost you the wait.

Or wait until a time on the clock. A timeout does not have to be counted in seconds. The small box that asks for the seconds — it opens when you add the line (step 1, then drag the new line up to just after the line it should follow), and again from right-click → [en:tran:Change Timing] on that line — has a chooser at its left: switch it from [en:tran:Seconds] to [en:tran:At Time] and type the time you want the run to move on — 7:05 AM, 8:30 PM. The line then reads ⏱ Next: Timeout (7:05 AM), and the pill counts down in minutes and hours (4:58, 1:12:30) instead of a long number of seconds. Use it for the notice board before a service: put it on the last announcement and the run leaves it exactly when the service starts, whether you armed it an hour or five minutes before. Its menu entry is [en:tran:Change Timing] rather than [en:tran:Change Seconds], and it opens on whichever half you armed it with — the two are alternatives, so choosing one clears the other. If the time you set has already gone by, the app says so ([en:tran:The set time is already due]) and starts nothing: it will not quietly wait until tomorrow. Set a new time, or arm it in seconds.

It counts only in the preview panel. A Next: line means something only while that presenting flow's preview panel is open (W-22b) — that panel is what walks the running order: clicking the line there starts its countdown, and a small pill at the panel's top-right shows the seconds left, with ⊗ to stop it and ⏸ to hold it. Click the line with the panel closed and the app says so ([en:tran:Open the presenting flow preview to use this action]) rather than looking as though it did something. It never goes to a screen, so it has no [en:tran:Apply on Screens] and no [en:tran:Set Specific Screen], and nothing can be attached to it.

A timeout can also ride along with another line. Attach it to a line — a slide, a song, a verse — as a CC element (W-22g), and that line means "show this, and go on by yourself N seconds later". Add the [en:tran:Next: Timeout] once, right-click the line you want it on → [en:tran:Add CC Elements] and pick it. Keep the Next: Timeout line itself in the list, though: a CC points at that line rather than copying it, so removing the line removes every follower of it as well (park it with [en:tran:Disable] if the run should not stop there — its followers still fire). Attached to a whole SONG it rides every slide of it, which is how a song advances by itself.

Each line may wait for its own length. First create a timeout if there is none: right-click the presenting flow's own name → [en:tran:Add Action] → [en:tran:Next: Timeout] and enter its seconds. Right-click each line that needs a wait → [en:tran:Add CC Elements] and pick that timeout. It appears as an indented CC row under each line it is attached to. A CC line normally reads whatever the Next: Timeout line is set to, so re-arming that one line re-arms every follower of it at once. When one line needs a different wait, click the small stopwatch at the right of that CC line — the indented row under the line, not the line itself (or right-click that CC line → [en:tran:Change Timing]) and answer with seconds or a time of day, exactly as on a line of its own. That answer belongs to that attachment only: the same Next: Timeout can hold the welcome slide for 4 seconds and the notice slide for 30, with one timeout in the running order instead of one per length. A row holding its own wait shows the stopwatch filled and reads its own number; one still following the element shows it hollow. To hand a row back, right-click it → [en:tran:Use Element Timing] — it goes back to the element's number and moves with it again.

If the run stopped moving on by itself, one of three things happened. You went somewhere yourself — clicked another line, or pressed the next key — and that calls a timeout off. Or the preview panel was closed: no Next: line counts without it. Or the run reached the end of the list. To set it going again, click the Next: line (or the line it rides on) in the preview panel.

workflows.title: Loop a set of slides, stop the loop, and jump back (Next: Interval, Jump to)
steps: Right-click the presenting flow itself — its own row in the list, not the empty part of the list and not one of its lines — and choose [en:tran:Add Action] → [en:tran:Next: Interval]. It asks how many [en:tran:Seconds], and the answer is part of the line; right-click the line → [en:tran:Change Seconds] to change it. Like every Next: line it works only while the preview panel is open (W-22b).

[en:tran:Next: Interval] keeps going. It moves the run on every so many seconds — a loop of announcement slides before the service. Going somewhere yourself does not stop it, it starts the count again from there, so a line you step to by hand gets the whole interval rather than the second that was left of the last one. To stop it, click the ⊗ ([en:tran:Stop Auto Next]) on the pill it puts at the top-right of the preview panel (it shows the seconds left, in the same colour as the line that started it); the ⏸ on the same pill ([en:tran:Pause Auto Next]) holds the count where it is until you press it again. Closing the panel stops it too, as does reaching the end of the sheet.

[en:tran:Next: Clear Interval] stops that loop, and it is the one way the SHEET can stop it: the pill, closing the panel and the end of the list are all you being at the machine. Add it — it asks nothing, there being only ever one clock running — and the line reads ⊘ Next: Clear Interval in the interval's own colour, because it is that same thing undone.
